articles.title: How I Stopped Overthinking at 2AM (And Finally Found Peace)
articles.summary: A cozy, honest short story about a sleepless night, a yellow mug of tea, and three gentle questions that made overthinking feel lighter.
articles.html:
My brain is running a marathon it never trained for.

It’s 2AM. My room is dark. My tea is cold. And the questions keep coming:

Why did I say that today?

Does Zoe think I was rude?

What if I fail tomorrow?

What if I never figure it out?

You know that voice, right? The one that gets louder when the world gets quiet.

The night I made my thoughts tea

For years, I thought overthinking meant something was wrong with me. That I was broken. That I had to fix my brain.

I tried telling myself, just don’t think about it.

It never worked. You can’t tell a storm to stop raining.

Then one night, at 2:13 AM, I tried something different.

Instead of fighting my thoughts, I made them tea.

I know. It sounds silly. But I got up, took my yellow mug with the little pink hearts, and said out loud:

“Okay, brain. I see you. You’re scared. Let’s talk.”

I didn’t argue. I didn’t judge. I let my thoughts sit next to me like a friend who showed up uninvited but clearly needed company.

It was awkward at first. My thoughts talked over each other, and twice I reached for my phone just to escape them. But I stayed for one cup of tea. That was all I asked of myself.

Paper, not phone

Then I wrote every thought down. On paper, not on my phone.

I’m scared I said something stupid today.

I’m scared people don’t like the real me.

I’m scared my future won’t get better.

On paper, they looked smaller. Less like monsters, more like worries. Just human worries.

I remembered something then.

When I was little, I woke up scared one night, and Mom came in. She didn’t say “stop worrying.” She didn’t say anything. She just sat on the edge of my bed until my breathing slowed.

I had forgotten that. Maybe that’s what I was trying to do with the tea. Sit on the edge of my own bed.

The text from Zoe

The next night, my phone buzzed. It was Zoe, my best friend, the one with a pencil always tucked into her curls and a tiny gold star pinned to every cardigan.

“Can’t sleep again. I keep thinking everyone secretly finds me annoying. Ugh. Tell me I’m being dramatic.”

I didn’t send her an argument. I typed:

“You’re not annoying. You’re tired. You’ve been carrying a lot. Come over, I’ll make tea.”

I hit send. Then I sat very still.

I had never talked to myself like that. Not once.

The three questions

That’s when I came up with the three questions I now ask every night. I wrote them on a card and tucked it inside my notebook:

  1. Is this true, or is this my fear talking?Most of the time, it’s fear. Not fact.
  2. Can I do something about this right now?If yes, I write one tiny step for tomorrow. If no, I tell my brain: “We’ll handle this tomorrow at 10AM. Not now.”
  3. What would I say to Zoe if she told me this?I’d never call her stupid. I’d say: “You’re tired. You’re doing your best. Let’s sleep.”

· · ·

The night it didn’t work

I’d like to tell you it worked perfectly.

It didn’t.

Two weeks later, I sat up at 3AM with the tea, the paper, and the three questions. And nothing worked.

The tea had gone cold. The page stayed blank. Every answer I wrote sounded like a lie, and the clock kept glowing: 3:07, then 3:12, then 3:19.

I felt like a fraud. All those calm nights, and here I was, right back at the beginning. I almost threw the notebook across the room.

Instead, I texted Zoe: “It’s not working tonight.”

She wrote back in seconds: “It doesn’t have to work every night. Some nights, you just sit with it. That counts too.”

So I did. I didn’t fix anything. I didn’t answer a single question. I just sat there, next to my thoughts, the way Mom once sat next to me.

Somewhere near 4AM, the window turned from black to deep blue. Eventually, I slept.

In the morning, the mug was still on the nightstand, the tea cold, the notebook open to a blank page. I looked at it for a while and decided it could stay there.

My night routine now

  • A mug of warm tea, and no phone for 30 minutes before bed
  • Paper on the nightstand: dump every thought, no filter
  • The three questions, then close the notebook and say: “We’re done for tonight.”

It isn’t perfect. Some nights I still overthink. But now I have a place to put my thoughts, instead of carrying them in my chest.

· · ·

If you’re reading this at 2AM with a busy brain:

You’re a person with a big heart and a mind that cares a little too much.

Make it some tea. Write it down. Tell a friend if you can.

And let yourself rest.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Checking My Phone 10 Times Before Sleep
articles.summary: Lina counts every phone check with hair ties, then sends a sarcastic message to the wrong chat and finds out who is really listening.
articles.html:
It’s 11:40 PM, and I’ve checked my phone nine times.

Nothing on it has changed.

I know it’s nine because I count with hair ties. One moves from my left wrist to my right every time I pick the phone up. Like a very sad abacus. I started three weeks ago, as a joke, to prove I wasn’t really checking that much.

The joke has not gone the way I planned.

Did they see it?

Who saw it?

What if Ms. Alvarez saw it?

The message that wasn’t for them

Here’s what I did. Our history group chat has five students and, since last Thursday, Ms. Alvarez, who was added “to see our progress.”

At 8:15, Marcus asked who was making the timeline slides. My thumbs answered before my brain could stop them:

“Sure, I’ll just do all of it. Again.”

It was meant for Zoe, in our other thread, the one where we complain about everything. I opened the wrong one.

I deleted it in twenty seconds. That sounds like a rescue until you see what’s left behind: a gray line that says This message was deleted. It’s like erasing a sentence from a chalkboard and leaving a perfectly clean rectangle. Everyone knows something was there.

Check number ten

At 11:52, I checked again. “Read by 4.”

No replies. Four people had seen the gray rectangle, four people had said nothing, and my brain turned that silence into a full trial. Jury. Judge. A very disappointed bailiff.

So I did the responsible thing. I put the phone on the dresser, all the way across the room.

At 12:10, I walked over there “to check the time.”

The time was on my phone. That’s the whole problem. My left wrist was bare by then, so I counted the rest on my fingers, which isn’t a system. It’s a confession.

· · ·

The question the screen couldn’t answer

Around 12:30, lying in the dark with the phone glowing across the room like a tiny, judgmental nightlight, I noticed something.

The screen could tell me who had read the message. It could never tell me what any of them thought.

For that, I’d have to ask an actual person. Terrible idea. Also the only one on offer.

I didn’t text Zoe. She’d been up at dawn all week, and I wasn’t going to drop one more thing into her phone at midnight. I’d say it out loud.

Then I fell asleep the way a phone dies at one percent: no warning, still holding on.

Eucalyptus and a half-eaten bagel

Zoe showed up at the bus stop with a pencil tucked in her curls, a tiny gold star pinned to her cardigan, and a smell of eucalyptus and wet cardboard. She’s been working mornings at her aunt’s flower shop since the holiday rush, and she carries it around like a very green rumor.

“I did something dumb,” I said, before I could rehearse it. I told her everything: the message, the wrong thread, the gray rectangle.

Zoe stopped chewing. “I muted that chat on Sunday. I haven’t read a single thing.”

Relief started climbing up my spine. Then she frowned.

“Wait. ‘Again’?”

“It was a joke.”

“About me?”

“About the slides. About… okay, a little about you.”

“I did the maps for the last project, Lina. By myself. At my kitchen table.” She said it flatly, not loud, and that was worse. “And if you were drowning, you could’ve just asked me. I’d have said yes.”

“I didn’t want to add to your pile,” I said. “You’ve been so tired.”

“Deciding I’m too busy isn’t the same as asking me.” She let that sit for a second, then sighed. “But thank you for telling me. I’m still a little mad.”

“That’s fair.”

“It’s very fair.” Her curls were sliding out of their clip. “Mine snapped in the flower cooler. Can I borrow one?”

She was already tugging a blue hair tie off my right wrist. She twisted her curls into a puff and looked at the bare spot on my arm. “Does this mess up your count?”

“Honestly? I think it helps.”

· · ·

What the chat said (and didn’t)

Before first period, I wrote to the whole group: That deleted message was sarcasm meant for someone else, and it wasn’t fair to any of you. I’ll make the timeline slides if someone can take sources.

My thumb hovered over Send for an embarrassingly long time.

Marcus replied in under a minute with a thumbs-up and “tbh I thought it was funny.” Priya sent a heart. Tessa said nothing. Ms. Alvarez said nothing either, but at the end of class she paused at my desk and said, “Looking forward to the timeline,” in a voice so ordinary I almost didn’t know what to do with it.

Tessa stayed quiet all day. I don’t know what that silence meant. Maybe nothing. Maybe she just doesn’t answer group chats.

By fifth period, I was doing math. Tessa had seen my apology before first period. It was now almost two. That was nearly six hours of silence, which my brain converted, with great confidence, into a verdict.

I stared at the back of her head for most of the lesson. She was drawing a lopsided cactus in her margin, and at one point she laughed at something Marcus whispered, a small, ordinary laugh that had nothing to do with me.

Or maybe it did. That was the hard part. A person can laugh and still be quietly upset, or laugh and be completely fine, and no amount of staring would tell me which. Only asking would. I wasn’t brave enough for that today.

So I wrote talk to Tessa? on the back of my hand, in pen. It looked like a very small, very honest reminder.

At lunch, I checked once, moved one hair tie, and put the phone in my bag. The afternoon went on without a verdict.

That night, I checked three times. I’m not going to pretend it was zero.

Three hair ties on my right wrist. One in Zoe’s curls. And my phone charging in the dark, doing nothing at all.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Night I Thought Everyone Hated Me (And They Didn’t)
articles.summary: Lina overhears her name through a half-open door and builds a full case against herself overnight. The next day, she asks.
articles.html:
The sentence was only seven words long, and by midnight I had turned it into a documentary.

Here is what happened. On Wednesday, after the winter fair meeting in Room 114, I realized my scarf was still hanging on the back of my chair, so I went back for it. The door was open about three inches, the kind of gap that lets sound out but doesn’t let people in. And through it, I heard Priya say, “I can’t believe she did that today.”

Then laughter. Not one person. Several.

I stood in the hallway with my hand halfway to the door, and I did what any brave, mature person would do. I turned around and left the scarf.

It was twenty-eight degrees outside. I walked the whole way home with my hands pulled up inside my sleeves, composing a speech to nobody, and every streetlight I passed felt like it was shining on a person who had Done Something.

The case against me

Okay, so you need the background. About an hour earlier, I had knocked a full jar of silver glitter onto the donation box. All of it. The box looked like it had been dipped in a disco. The room went completely silent, and I said, in a voice I didn’t recognize, “Well. The fair is now officially sparkly.” Nobody laughed. Dev raised his eyebrows. Priya looked at her notebook. Someone coughed. We moved on to hot chocolate.

So when I heard that sentence through the door, my brain did not ask what it meant. My brain opened a courtroom.

That night, I lay in bed as both the prosecutor and the defendant, and the prosecutor was winning. Exhibit A: Dev’s eyebrows. Exhibit B: Priya not looking up. Exhibit C: nobody asked me to stay and stack chairs, which, in committee terms, is basically a public shunning.

Around one in the morning, I noticed something strange about my evidence. Every piece of it was a look, a pause, or something that had not happened. Nobody had said anything cruel to me. My entire case rested on eyebrows and silence.

I also played the sentence back about forty times, trying different tones, like a detective with a very small tape recorder. I can’t believe she did that today, said with admiration. I can’t believe she did that today, said with a sigh. I can’t believe she did that today, said by someone handing out a very tiny trophy. All forty versions were possible. That is the annoying thing about seven words: they don’t come with a tone, and my brain, handed a blank, always fills it in with the cruelest option on the menu.

That should have been the end of the trial. It was not. The prosecutor simply argued that silence was the cleverest kind of cruelty. (She is very good.)

· · ·

Zoe’s hands

In the morning, I found Zoe at her locker with my opening statement fully prepared. I got exactly five words in.

“Zoe, I think the whole committee—”

“Can we do this later?” She wasn’t looking at me. She was holding her audition sheet, and it was shaking, just slightly, like a leaf in a very polite wind. “I’m sorry. I know you’re having a thing. But my audition is at 3:15, and I think I might throw up on the piano.”

I had a speech about the committee. It was a good speech. I folded it up and put it in my pocket.

“Okay,” I said. “Give me your hands.”

She gave me her hands. They were freezing. We stood there next to locker 212 while a freshman struggled with the one beside us, and I discovered that it is very hard to hold on to a full-blown conspiracy theory while someone’s fingers are cold.

“You’re going to be great,” I said. It wasn’t advice. It was just the only true thing I had on me.

· · ·

Seven words

At lunch, Priya was at the end of a cafeteria table, peeling a clementine. My knees felt like they belonged to someone else. But somewhere between the locker and the lunch line, I had noticed something. Zoe had said exactly what she needed, out loud, with her hands shaking, and it had worked better than any speech I owned. I could try one honest sentence.

“Hi,” I said. “So, I went back for my scarf last night, and the door was open, and I heard you say my name. I didn’t hear the rest. I just took the worst version home.”

Priya stopped peeling. Her face went through confusion, then horror, then something close to a groan.

“Oh no. Lina. We were laughing about the glitter.”

“The glitter.”

“Dev said the donation box looked like it had been to a rave, and I said I couldn’t believe you did that today, because you just stood there covered in sparkle and announced the fair was officially sparkly. It was the best thing anyone has said in that room all year. We were trying so hard not to laugh in front of you, because you looked mortified. Then you left, and we completely lost it.”

I thought about that for a second. “That might be the least helpful kindness in history.”

“Yeah,” Priya said, wincing. “We’re going to work on it.”

It wasn’t a perfect ending. Dev still couldn’t explain his eyebrows, and some mysteries stay mysteries. But my scarf was waiting on the back of my chair in Room 114, exactly where I had left it, and a small, careful part of my chest unclenched.

· · ·

At 3:15, I sat on the floor outside the music room with the scarf in my lap, listening through a door that was open about three inches. A piano started. It hit one wrong note, stopped, and then kept going.

This time, I stayed for the whole song.

When I looked down, there was still a little silver glitter stuck to the pink heart on my sweater, catching the light from the hallway window. I didn’t brush it off.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: Why My Brain Gets Loud at Night (and Quiet in the Morning)
articles.summary: Awake at 4 a.m., Lina knocks on the neighborhood bakery door and ends up shaping sixty rolls for a baker with loud nights of his own.
articles.html:
At 4:10 in the morning, I was standing on the back steps of Haddad’s Bakery in pajama pants, my school coat and one mismatched sock, holding a library book as an excuse.

The book was due Thursday. This was not a library emergency. But the bakery light had been on every night that week, and I had been awake to see it every night that week, and at some point around 3:50 my brain had said, very calmly, go ask the person who is awake why he is awake.

I had already tried the usual things. I counted backward from a hundred. I recited the nine slides in my head, and I made it to slide four before the dog showed up. I rearranged my pillow into four separate positions, none of which was a position a human being could sleep in.

Two of me

Okay, so here is my problem. At 11 p.m., my brain turns its volume all the way up. On Friday I had a river-cleanup presentation (four minutes, nine slides, one very large chart), and every night that week my brain had played it like a movie, with new disasters added each time. The projector dies. My voice cracks. A dog walks in.

Then, at 7 a.m., the volume drops to nothing. Morning me eats toast and thinks, What presentation? It’s four minutes. Morning me has never once believed night me. That is the part that makes me furious. We live in the same body, and we don’t even talk.

The back door opened. Mr. Haddad was a large man with flour up to both elbows and a pencil behind his ear, and he looked at me, then at the book, then at the clock over the oven.

“You’re Lina from number nine,” he said. “It’s four o’clock.”

“I know. I brought a book.”

“Why?”

“I honestly don’t know.”

He considered this. Then he said, “Can you shape rolls?”

“I can… learn?”

“Good. Danny didn’t come in, and I have sixty to finish before six.” He held the door wider. “I’m not being kind. I’m behind. I need hands.”

· · ·

Sixty rolls

The bakery was the warmest place I had ever been at that hour. A radio played something low and crackly, and the whole room smelled like the inside of a loaf. Steel racks lined the walls like bookshelves for bread. Mr. Haddad showed me once: cut, round, tuck. Cut, round, tuck. My first ten rolls looked like small, sad potatoes.

“Again,” said Mr. Haddad, which turned out to be the only feedback he gave. Not “good,” not “bad.” Just “again,” like a very patient metronome.

I had assumed the loudness would stay outside the door. It did not.

“The projector dies,” my brain announced, right over the hum of the mixer. “Your voice cracks. A dog.”

“Your face is doing something,” Mr. Haddad said, not looking up.

“My brain is loud.”

He nodded, like I had told him it was drizzling. “Mine too. Around two. It doesn’t come with an off switch.”

I rounded a roll. “I have a theory,” I said. “I think night me is the real me, and morning me is a liar who just feels better because the sun is out.”

He laughed so hard he had to set down his tray. “Which one told you that?”

“The night one.”

“Then I would say,” said Mr. Haddad, wiping his eyes with a floury wrist, “that the night one is biased.”

I waited for the rest of the answer. There wasn’t one. When I asked him why the nights were louder, he shrugged and said, “Might be the quiet. Might be tired. Might be both. I just know I’d rather be up with something to do with my hands.” He said it like a fact about weather, not like advice, and I decided not to turn it into advice.

· · ·

I wish I could tell you the volume dropped to zero. It didn’t. It rose and fell like the radio. But somewhere around roll thirty, I noticed something small: I was counting rolls instead of dogs.

That was the entire miracle. One tray, maybe two. It was not a cure or a trick, just a tray of rolls and, for the length of it, a dog who stayed out of the room. At 5:20 the projector came back for a full minute, and I let it, and kept tucking.

At 5:30, the last tray had to rise, and nothing in the world can make dough hurry. Mr. Haddad poured himself a coffee and made me a mug of hot water with honey, because, he said, it was the middle of the night and I was a minor. We sat on two flour sacks and watched the trays do nothing at all. It was the first time all week I had watched something do nothing without feeling responsible for it.

By 5:50, forty-one of the rolls on the rack were mine. Thirteen of them looked like actual rolls. Mr. Haddad slid a paper bag across the counter, still warm enough that I could feel it through my coat.

“Payment,” he said.

“For the presentation?”

“For the labor. The presentation you’re on your own for.”

· · ·

Outside, the sky had gone the color of dishwater, the good kind. I walked home slowly with the bag against my ribs and watched the streetlights switch off one by one down the block, like someone going through a house, making sure everything was fine.

Friday still had a projector in it. It might still have a dog. I had no answer about my brain and its two schedules, only a bakery, a baker with a loud night of his own, and a bag of bread.

I sat down on the curb in front of number nine and ate the first roll I had ever made. It was lopsided. It was still warm. I would not have believed it at 11 p.m., but it was one of the best things I had ever eaten.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Learned to Sleep Without Saying Sorry in My Head
articles.summary: Lina apologizes to a barista, a revolving door and a phone charger before midnight, until a jam jar teaches her which sorrys actually have an address.
articles.html:
By midnight, I had apologized to eleven people, and I hadn’t said a word to any of them.

It happened the way it always happens. I turned off the lamp, pulled the blue quilt up to my chin, and my brain switched on like a shop that only opens after dark. Its first customer was the barista from that morning.

I had asked for a lid. Then, half a second later, I had asked for a sleeve too. He’d said, “No problem,” and slid the cup across the counter without even looking up.

Sorry. Sorry, I know that’s two things. Sorry.

He had said no problem. I had heard him say no problem. But my brain filed it under polite, probably lying and opened a new folder.

Was I rude?

Did I take too long?

Who else did I bother today?

The department of small apologies

Here is the list my brain read out to me, in order. I’m not exaggerating. I wrote it down afterward because I didn’t believe it myself.

Sorry to the barista, for the sleeve. Sorry to Ms. Alvarez, for walking in two minutes late, even though the bell hadn’t rung. Sorry to a girl on the bus, for existing near her backpack. Sorry to my mom, for asking her to sign a form. Sorry to a revolving door, because I’d pushed it too hard and it had made a noise. Sorry to my phone charger, which I had stepped on.

The charger made me laugh, a little, in the dark. It was the first useful thing that happened all night.

Because for the first time, I could hear how it sounded. Most of those sorrys weren’t about people. They were a reflex, like a hiccup. Every time I took up a little space in the world, something inside me whispered sorry before anyone had asked.

And I was exhausted. I had spent the whole day being careful and polite, and then I’d spent the whole night billing myself for it.

A jar with an address

The next afternoon, I told Zoe. She was sitting on the library steps with a pencil in her curls and a tiny gold star pinned to her cardigan, eating clementine segments one at a time like a very serious jeweler.

“So you apologized to a charger,” she said.

“It was an accident!”

“Lina, it’s a charger.” She wasn’t mocking me. She said it gently, the way you’d tell someone about to leap over a puddle that it’s only a puddle. “Also, yesterday you said sorry to the revolving door. I was behind you. I heard it.”

“It made a noise.”

“It’s a door. Noise is its whole job.”

I put my head on my knees. Zoe waited, which is one of her best skills, and then she pulled a clean jam jar out of her bag. It still smelled faintly like strawberries and eucalyptus.

“My aunt gives these to everyone at the flower shop,” she said. “Tonight, write each sorry on its own slip of paper. Don’t think. Just write. Then put them all in the jar and go to sleep.”

“And then?”

“Then, in the morning, you sort them into two piles. Real and reflex. And here’s the only rule.” She held up a clementine segment like a tiny gavel. “A real sorry has an address. There’s a person it belongs to, and there’s one small thing you can actually do about it. If it has no address, it doesn’t get delivered.”

· · ·

Nineteen slips

That night I wrote nineteen slips. It took eleven minutes, and the strange part was how much quieter my head got with every one. I had been carrying all those sorrys like a stack of heavy plates. Setting them down, one at a time, felt like unloading a bus.

The next morning, I sat on my bedroom floor with the jar and my yellow mug, and I made two piles.

Pile one: Real. Pile two: Reflex.

The barista went in Reflex. So did the bus girl, the revolving door, and the charger. By the time I’d finished, Reflex had seventeen slips, and the pile looked like a very small snowdrift.

Real had two.

The first was Priya’s math notebook. I’d borrowed it on Monday, and it had been sitting in my bag for four days. That one had an address. I wrote to her: “I forgot to bring your notebook. I’ll have it tomorrow. Thank you for waiting.” I noticed I hadn’t typed the word “sorry” at all, and it still felt kind. Priya replied in under a minute: “lol I forgot you had it. thanks!!”

The second slip was the hard one. On Tuesday, in our science group, Dev had suggested we build our model volcano out of a cereal box, and I had said, in a voice that came out sharper than I meant, “That’s a dumb idea.” He’d gone quiet. I had pretended not to notice, and then I’d gone home and apologized to a charger instead of to him.

That one had an address, too. And it did not fit in a text message.

I found Dev at the science table before first period. My hands were cold. I said, “On Tuesday, I called your idea dumb. It wasn’t. I was stressed, and I took it out on you. I’m sorry.”

Dev blinked at me for a second. “Oh,” he said. “Okay. Thanks.” Then, after a moment, he added, “Honestly, it was a little dumb. But thanks.”

We both laughed. It was a small, ordinary laugh. And it did something eleven nights of silent apologizing had never done: it was over.

The night the jar wasn’t enough

I’d love to tell you that was the end of it. It wasn’t.

Three weeks later, at 1 AM, I was apologizing again, this time to a teacher I had accidentally interrupted. The slips came out like a flood, and the jar was too small, and after seven of them I just stopped and sat on the edge of the bed with my face in my hands. Nothing sorted. Nothing felt like it had an address. It all just felt like me, and all of me felt wrong.

I texted Zoe: “The jar isn’t working tonight.”

She wrote back in seconds: “It doesn’t have to work every night. What did you do today that was kind?”

I thought about it. I had held a door for a stranger, without apologizing to it. I’d lent my pencil case to a girl in homeroom. I had said “thank you” to the bus driver, and he’d smiled.

I put the half-filled jar on the nightstand and said, quietly, to the ceiling, “Thank you for today.” To whom, I don’t know. Maybe to me.

That was enough to sleep on.

Now the jar sits next to my bed, about a third full. Some nights I fill it. Some nights I just look at it, and my brain goes quiet, like a dog that has seen the leash.

I still say sorry when I should. I just make sure it has an address.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The 3AM Thought That Wasn’t True
articles.summary: At 3:07 AM, a calm, certain thought tells Lina everyone saw her fail. A two-column notebook page and a small card in a drawer teach her how to ask it for ID.
articles.html:
At 3:07 AM, a thought walked into my room and sat on my chest like it paid rent.

It didn’t knock. It didn’t whisper. It spoke in the calm, certain voice of a news anchor reading the weather.

“Everyone at the art fair meeting saw that you have no idea what you’re doing.”

That was it. One sentence. And my whole body believed it, from the tips of my toes to the very back of my ears, which had turned hot in the dark.

Did they notice?

Did Ms. Alvarez notice?

Do I even belong on this committee?

A thought in a suit

Here is what had happened that Tuesday. At the art fair meeting, we were splitting up jobs, and Ms. Alvarez asked who was ordering the paint. I said, “Oh, I’ll do it,” and then, ten minutes later, I realized I had no idea how many jars we needed, which colors, or who to ask. I looked at my notebook for a long time, as if the answer might be hiding in the margins.

That was all. Nobody gasped. Nobody even looked up.

But at 3:07 in the morning, my brain took that tiny, ordinary moment and dressed it in a suit. A very serious one, with a tie. And a thought wearing a suit sounds like a fact.

That’s the trick, I realized. It isn’t the words. It’s the voice. At 3 AM, every thought sounds like it has been to law school.

So I did something I had never done before. I turned on the lamp, picked up my notebook, and asked it for identification.

Cross-examining a thought

I drew two columns, because I remembered a trick from science class. The left one said What I actually know. The right one said What I’m guessing.

Left column: I said I’d order the paint. I didn’t know how many jars. I looked at my notebook.

Right column: Everyone noticed. Everyone thinks I’m clueless. Ms. Alvarez is disappointed.

I stared at the page. The left side was three short sentences. The right side was a whole movie, with a plot, a villain and a sad violin.

“Excuse me,” I said to the room, very quietly, “what evidence do you have?”

The thought didn’t answer. Thoughts at 3 AM never do. They just keep sitting there looking confident.

So I added a third line at the bottom of the page, in pen: Nothing new has happened since 8 PM. Only the volume has changed.

It didn’t make the thought disappear. But it made it smaller, like a coat on a chair that looks like a person until you turn on the light.

· · ·

What Zoe was hiding

At school the next day, I found Zoe by the art room sinks with a pencil in her curls and a tiny gold star pinned to her cardigan, scrubbing blue paint off her thumb.

“Okay, strange question,” I said. “On Tuesday, did I look like I had no idea what I was doing?”

Zoe stopped scrubbing. She looked at me for a long moment, the way you look at someone who has just asked if the sky is still up.

“Lina. You forgot the paint order.”

My stomach dropped. “I knew it.”

“Dev forgot the tape. Priya forgot her notebook. I forgot my own name tag, and I wrote it on my hand in marker, and then I washed my hand.” She held up her thumb, as proof. “Also, Priya cried in the supply closet for ten minutes. We all pretended not to hear.”

“Wait. What?”

“Nobody had any idea what they were doing. That’s why it’s called a committee.”

I laughed. It came out of me in a wobbly, surprised way, like air from a balloon. All night, I had been defending myself against a jury that had been busy forgetting its own tape.

After school, I asked Ms. Alvarez how many jars we needed. She said, “Twelve, and thank you for asking.” She didn’t look disappointed. She looked like someone who had twelve other things to think about.

The night it came back

I’d love to tell you the thought never returned. It did.

Two weeks later, at 3:12 AM, it walked in again, same suit, same tie, same calm voice. Only the sentence was different: “You’ll mess up the art fair, and everyone will remember.”

I reached for the notebook. I drew the two columns. And I got stuck. My left column was empty, because nothing had happened yet. My right column kept filling up on its own, faster than I could write. I felt the old panic climbing up my throat.

I texted Zoe: “It’s back. I can’t cross-examine it. There’s nothing to cross-examine.”

She replied in under a minute, which meant she was awake too: “Then don’t. Say hi. Write what it is on a card. Put it in a drawer. It can wait there until daylight.”

I tore a small card from the back of my notebook. I wrote, in my neatest handwriting, Not a fact. A 3 AM. Then I folded it in half and put it in the nightstand drawer, next to a pen with no ink and a lonely hair tie.

I closed the drawer, gently, the way you close the door of a room where someone is finally asleep.

The thought was still there, a little. But it was quieter, like a radio in another apartment. I lay down. I breathed. At some point I stopped listening.

These days, the drawer holds seven cards. In the morning, I read them over tea, and each one looks smaller in daylight. One says Not a fact. A 3 AM. Another says Not a fact. A tired brain. The newest one just says Hi.

I still get thoughts at 3 AM. I just ask for their ID now.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Replaying Conversations at Night
articles.summary: After saying “interesting” about a friend’s drawing, Lina replays lunch fourteen times in the dark. One replay, two short sentences and a sticky note that says “Roll credits” help her stop.
articles.html:
At 11:48 PM, I pressed play on a conversation that had ended nine hours earlier.

It was a tiny one. At lunch, Dev had shown me his drawing of a lighthouse, and I had said, “Oh. It’s… interesting.” He smiled with only half of his face and said, “Yeah. Thanks.” Then he put the drawing back in his folder and went quiet.

That was all. Eleven seconds, maybe.

But in the dark, my mind loaded it like a movie and hit play. Interesting. His half smile. The folder closing. Play.

Why did I say interesting?

Did he hear it as an insult?

What if I had said beautiful instead?

The director’s cut

Here is the strange part. I didn’t just replay it. I edited it.

In take two, I said, “Wow, the lighthouse is great!” In take three, I said it with a bigger smile. In take five, I gave a whole speech about the shading, which I had not noticed at all. By take nine, I had written Dev a heartfelt apology and an award.

None of those takes were real. The only real take was the first one, and I couldn’t change it, no matter how many times I rewound.

By 1:15 AM, I had watched it fourteen times. My stomach felt like I had eaten a whole bag of paperclips. And the weirdest thing was that the movie had not gotten any better. Replaying it didn’t fix a single frame. It just made me tired.

That’s when I noticed something. A replay never ends with a decision. It ends with another replay.

· · ·

Fourteen takes

The next day, I told Zoe everything. She listened with a sandwich in one hand and her pencil, as always, tucked in her curls.

“Wait,” she said. “How many times did you watch it?”

“Fourteen.”

She counted on her fingers, slowly, as if she needed the evidence. “And did the movie change?”

“…No.”

“Then you’re not studying it, Lina. You’re just rewatching it, hoping the ending changes.”

I opened my mouth to argue, and then I closed it, because she was right. She gave me a tiny, kind shrug. “One replay is a lesson. Fourteen is a habit.”

So we made a rule, right there on the steps, with crumbs on our knees. I would get one replay. Just one. And when it finished, I had to write two short sentences on paper: What did actually happen? and What is one small thing I can do tomorrow?

Not a speech. Not an apology. Just one small thing.

What Dev was thinking

That afternoon, I walked up to Dev at the lockers. My knees were doing a strange little dance.

“Hey,” I said. “About your lighthouse. I said ‘interesting’ yesterday, and I think it came out weird. I really like the sky. The part with the little stars.”

Dev blinked. “Oh! You did? I wasn’t even…” He laughed, a little embarrassed. “Honestly, I was thinking about my dentist appointment. I went quiet because I had to leave early. I didn’t notice you said anything weird.”

“So you weren’t upset?”

“Lina. I was thinking about a tooth.”

Evidence, again, in the daylight. I had been rewinding a movie in which I was the only person who cared about the plot.

Then he held up his folder and said, “Do you want to see the other one? I drew a second lighthouse.” And we looked at it together, and it really was interesting, in the best way.

Roll credits

I’d love to tell you the replays stopped forever. They didn’t.

Three weeks later, I said something silly during a group presentation and heard it again at 11:32 PM, loud and clear, with a close-up of my own face. The projector in my head clicked on. I felt it warming up.

But this time I took out my notebook. I let it play once, all the way through. Then I wrote my two sentences. What happened: I made a joke and two people laughed. One small thing: nothing. It was fine.

And then, because the movie wanted to start again, I did something new. I took a sticky note, wrote Roll credits on it, and pressed it on my lamp.

That’s it. That’s the whole trick. When the movie tries to start over, I look at the lamp and think, I already watched that one. The credits are rolling.

Sometimes it works right away. Sometimes I have to say it three times, like asking a very persistent cat to get off the keyboard. But the movie doesn’t get to play fourteen times anymore.

These days, my notebook has a page called Takes, and most of the entries are only two lines long. One of them says, Dev was thinking about a tooth. It’s my favorite.

I still replay conversations sometimes. I just stop at the credits now.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: My Brain’s Bedtime Stories Are Always Scary (Until I Changed Them)
articles.summary: Every night Lina’s brain reads her a scary story about tomorrow. With three index cards and a friend named Zoe, she learns that she is the author and gets to write a likelier ending.
articles.html:
Every night at 10:40, right after I turn off the lamp, my brain clears its throat and begins to read me a bedtime story.

It is never a nice one. It has a narrator with a very smooth voice, a dramatic soundtrack, and a plot I have heard so many times that I could recite it in my sleep, if only I could sleep.

That Sunday, the story was called Tomorrow’s Presentation.

“Once upon a time, Lina stood up in front of the whole class and forgot every single word. The silence lasted nine hours. Nobody ever forgot it. The end.”

The end. Like it was a fact.

What if I really do freeze?

What if my voice shakes and everyone hears?

What if it goes exactly like the story?

A narrator with a very smooth voice

Here is something I had never noticed before. The story was well told. It had details: my hands shaking, a cough from the back row, a clock ticking in the silence. A story with that many details feels like a memory. But it was not a memory. It had not happened. I had made it up, one scary page at a time.

My brain, it turns out, is an excellent author. It just only writes one genre.

I told Zoe about it the next morning, while we sat on the floor of the hallway with our backs against the lockers. She tilted her head, the pencil in her curls tilting with it.

“So you wrote a horror story,” she said, “and then you got scared of it.”

“…Yes?”

“Lina. That’s like building a haunted house and then being surprised you can’t sleep in it.”

I laughed, which was annoying, because I wanted to stay serious about my terror.

· · ·

Three endings

“Okay,” said Zoe, pulling a stack of index cards out of her backpack, as if she had been waiting all her life for this exact emergency. “Authors can edit. Give me three endings.”

“Three?”

“The scary one. The silly one. And the most likely one. Not the best one, not the worst one. The one that a boring, honest reporter would write.”

So we sat there with our cards and our colored pens.

The scary ending was easy. I had it memorized. On the silly one, Zoe suggested that a parrot flew in through the window and finished my presentation for me, which made me snort so hard I got hiccups. And then, slowly, I wrote the third one.

I will feel shaky. I will look at my notes. I will take one breath and keep going. It will not be perfect, and then it will be over.

I read it twice. It was a boring ending. It had no thunderstorm in it, no silence lasting nine hours. And it was, by far, the one that sounded the most like real life.

“See?” said Zoe. “A story needs a plot. Not a prophecy.”

The ending I put under my pillow

I wish I could tell you the scary story never came back. It did, the very next night. Same voice, same dramatic soundtrack. This time, though, I knew what to do. I turned on the lamp and took out my cards.

I did not argue with the story. I just picked up the third card, I will feel shaky, take one breath, and keep going, and read it aloud, in a boring reporter voice. Then I put it under my pillow, like a coin for a very tired fairy.

The scary narrator still tried to speak. But now, every time, I had a reply. Thanks. I have another ending.

The presentation, by the way, was fine. I stumbled over one word, I breathed, I kept going. Nobody coughed. Nobody remembered it for nine hours. Ms. Alvarez said, “Clear and calm,” and moved on to the next slide, and that was it.

I still have a shelf of cards. Some say Scary. Silly. Likely. and some just say Likely. My brain still tells me bedtime stories. They are just shorter now, and I am allowed to write the ending.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Comparing My Life to Everyone Else’s Highlights
articles.summary: Scrolling at night, Lina feels like everyone else is living a perfect life. Zoe’s messy camera roll and a notebook page called “behind the scenes” help her see the whole picture.
articles.html:
At 10:52 PM, I was lying in bed with my phone one inch from my nose, watching everyone else have a perfect Saturday.

Maya had been to a lake. Jonah had baked bread that had risen like it had somewhere important to be. Two girls from my grade sat on a rooftop in matching sweaters, laughing with their whole faces.

My own Saturday had been a pile of laundry, a library fine, and a sandwich eaten over the sink.

“Everyone is living their life. You are just waiting for yours.”

Why does everyone else seem so happy?

Am I the only one who feels behind?

What is wrong with my life?

A highlight reel against my whole movie

I told Zoe on Monday, and she did not say, “Don’t compare yourself.” I am grateful, because that sentence has never worked on anyone.

Instead, she said, “Can I see your phone?”

I handed it over, a little suspicious. Her own camera roll was a disaster: forty blurry pictures of her thumb, a cat that was mostly ear, a sandwich, another sandwich, and one photo of the sky taken, as she explained, “by accident, while crying about a math test.”

“This is my real Saturday,” she said. “You know what I posted?”

“The cat?”

“The one good photo of the cat. You see highlights. I see the other thirty-nine.”

I laughed so hard the boy in front of us turned around.

· · ·

Behind the scenes

That afternoon, on the library steps, Zoe drew a line down the middle of a notebook page. At the top of the left side she wrote What I want to take. On the right side she wrote What I actually take.

“Fill in the right side,” she said. “Not mean things. Just true things people never post.”

It was strange how fast the page filled up. Maya: the six photos where her eyes were closed. The long, boring drive to the lake. The sunburn. Jonah: the three loaves that didn’t rise. The rooftop girls: probably a fight about who got the better seat.

I looked at the page and felt something quiet settle in me. These were not lies. They were just the parts of life that never get a spotlight. My own Saturday, with its laundry and its sandwich over the sink, had been completely normal, which meant it was real.

My own two columns

I still scroll. But now I have a small habit: before I put the phone down, I ask, What is the behind-the-scenes of this picture?

And then I write one line in my own notebook, on a page I titled My real Saturday. Laundry. A good sandwich. I laughed at lunch. I finished my book.

Read back, it looks like a pretty good life, only without a filter.

Last week, Maya stopped me in the hallway and said, “I love your sweater. I always wish I could pull off blue.” I stared at her for a very long time. She had wished I had something. She, who had been to the lake.

It turns out everyone has a highlight reel, and everyone is watching someone else’s. I just stopped taking mine as the only measure.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Parked My Thoughts Before Sleep
articles.summary: Lina believes she cannot sleep until every problem is solved. A paper parking lot and a closing gate teach her to give each worry an address and a time, and let the night be for rest.
articles.html:
For three weeks, I had been going to bed with a mountain on my chest.

It wasn’t one problem. If it had been one, I could have handled it, probably. It was all of them: the science project, the library book I had lost, the group chat I hadn’t answered, the thing I said to my cousin at dinner, my math grade, and a small, mysterious squeak in my backpack.

My brain’s rule was simple: You are not allowed to sleep until everything is solved.

The trouble with that rule is that it is Monday night, 11:20, and almost nothing can be solved on a Monday night at 11:20. The library is closed. My cousin is asleep. The squeak is still squeaking.

What if I forget one of them?

What if I sleep and something falls apart?

When will I ever catch up?

You can’t fix a Tuesday problem on a Monday night

I tried to explain it all to Zoe at lunch. I talked for so long that her sandwich got lonely.

“Okay,” she said, when I finally ran out of breath. “Which of these can you fix tonight, at midnight, in your pajamas?”

I looked at my list. I thought about it honestly.

“…The squeak? Maybe.”

“And the rest?”

“No. The library opens at eight. My cousin wakes up at seven. The project is due Friday.”

“So,” said Zoe, “you’re staying awake all night to solve problems that are not available until morning.” She said it kindly, the way you tell a friend they have been wearing their sweater inside out all day.

Something in my chest loosened by exactly one notch.

· · ·

The parking lot

After school, Zoe unrolled a big sheet of paper on her bedroom floor and drew a rectangle with white lines. “This,” she announced, “is the Tomorrow Parking Lot.”

“Is it a game?”

“It’s a system. Every worry gets a parking space. Each space has a time, and a car that is not driving anywhere until then.”

We drew little cars, one for each problem. The library book got a small blue car parked at 8:00 AM. My cousin got a yellow one at after school, one kind text. The project got a green truck at Wednesday, one hour. Even the squeak got a tiny red car at Saturday, open the backpack.

I know it sounds silly, but as each car rolled into its space, something in me went quiet. The worry was not gone. It was parked. It had an address, a time, and a plan for when to come back.

“The lot closes at night,” said Zoe. “Cars don’t drive around at 11 PM. That’s the rule.”

Closing the gate

That night, I did it in my own notebook. I drew my own tiny parking lot, with six spaces and six little cars. It took seven minutes. When I finished, I drew a gate across the bottom of the page, the way you draw a fence, and I wrote underneath it: Lot closed until 8 AM.

I won’t pretend that my brain applauded. It tried, twice, to drive a car out of the lot. The library book was the loudest. Each time I said, quietly, “That one’s parked until eight,” and looked at the gate.

Somewhere between the second try and the third, I stopped counting cars and fell asleep.

In the morning, I found the library book under my bed, exactly where a book would be if a person had stopped checking for it at midnight. The cousin text took one sentence, and he replied with three hearts. The project took the whole of Wednesday. The squeak was a pencil sharpener.

I do not fix my whole life before I sleep anymore. I just park it. The cars are always there when I wake up. They are just much smaller in daylight.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Night I Realized Worrying Doesn’t Prevent Bad Things
articles.summary: Lina believes her worrying is what keeps her aunt’s plane in the air. A paper napkin airplane and one caring text message teach her that care is not the same as carrying.
articles.html:
My aunt Salma was flying to see us that Friday, and by Thursday night I had already crashed her plane about forty times.

Not really, of course. Only in my head. I lay in bed watching the tiny blinking lights of planes cross the dark, and I imagined everything that could go wrong: the storm, the engine, the turbulence, the long wait at the airport.

And behind all those pictures was a strange, stubborn belief that I had never said out loud, even to myself.

“If I keep worrying, she will be safe. If I stop, something will happen.”

It felt like a job. Like I was holding the plane up with my mind, and any second of relaxing could make me drop it.

What if I fall asleep and that’s the moment it matters?

Did your worrying hold the plane up?

At breakfast, Zoe found me staring at my cereal like it had insulted me. I told her everything, even the part where I felt ridiculous.

She picked up a paper napkin, folded it into a lopsided airplane, and held it up between two fingers. “Okay. I’m flying this one. Are you worrying it into the air?”

None of my forty crashes had changed one thing about the weather.

“…No,” I said. “It isn’t doing anything.”

“That’s what I thought.” She flew it gently across the table and landed it on my toast. “Worrying feels like love, Lina. But it isn’t a seatbelt. It just makes you the one who’s buckled in tight all night.”

· · ·

Care is not the same as carrying

That was the sentence I wrote on the back of my hand later, in pen: Care is not the same as carrying.

I do love my aunt. But loving someone and carrying their whole flight on your chest are two different things. One is warm. The other is just heavy.

So Zoe and I made a small rule. When I catch myself worrying about something I cannot control, I ask: Is there one caring thing I can actually do?

That night, there was. I took out my phone and wrote to Aunt Salma: Safe travels tomorrow. I made up the guest room. Can’t wait to see you. Love, Lina. I pressed send. It felt like a little paper airplane of my own.

Then came the harder part: I put the phone face down and let the plane be hers to fly.

The yarn in the basket

I still felt a pull, a little tug that said, just one more check. But now I knew what the tug was. It wasn’t information. It was a habit that looked like love.

I pictured the tangled ball of worry sitting in the yarn basket by my desk. Yarn is only useful when it’s knitted into something, not worn.

My aunt landed the next afternoon with a suitcase full of dates and a hug that smelled like the airport coffee shop. She had slept the whole way.

She had no idea about the forty crashes. The plane had needed a pilot, a runway, and a very sleepy passenger, not me.

I still worry about people I love. I just ask a different question now. Not how do I hold this up? but what is one caring thing I can do? Most nights the answer is a text, or just good night.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Needing to Be Perfect to Sleep
articles.summary: Lina keeps erasing the same line on her art fair drawing at midnight. Zoe’s lopsided clay mug and three “good enough” questions help her finish, add a gold star, and go to sleep.
articles.html:
At 11:55 PM, I erased the same line for the ninth time and watched a small gray pile of eraser crumbs grow on my desk.

It was a drawing for the art fair: a lighthouse on a hill, with a tiny window glowing at the top. The lighthouse was fine. The hill was fine. But the line of the roof was almost straight, and almost was not good enough.

That was my rule for the whole week: You may not sleep until this is perfect.

In real life it looked like a girl with red eyes, a worn-out eraser, and a sheet of paper that had started to go thin.

What if I hand it in and everyone sees the crooked roof?

What if it’s not good enough?

A perfect thing that never gets finished

The next day, I told Zoe, and she just pulled a lopsided lump of clay out of her backpack that was shaped, with some goodwill, like a mug.

“I made this on Saturday,” she said proudly. “It leans. The handle is huge. It holds exactly half a cup of tea.”

“It’s done,” said Zoe, and she set it on the bench between us like a trophy. “I use it every morning. You know what I don’t use? Anything still waiting to be perfect. That just sits in a drawer, glowing with potential.”

The leaning mug was, I realized, much more useful than my perfect lighthouse, which did not exist yet.

· · ·

Perfect doesn’t have a bedtime

“Here’s what I think,” she said. “Perfect never says ‘okay, that’s enough for tonight.’ Perfect has no bedtime. You need a different word.”

“Which word?” “Good enough.”

It sounded like giving up. But Zoe explained that good enough is not careless. It is a line that you draw, ahead of time, when your head is clear.

So we wrote three questions on a card, and I read them in the cafeteria until I knew them by heart:

  1. Is it clear? Could someone understand what I meant?
  2. Is it kind to the person who will see it? Is it honest and made with care?
  3. Is it done enough to rest? Would a tired friend call this finished?

If the answer to all three was yes, I was allowed to stop.

The little gold star

That night, at 9:30, with my tea still warm, I held the drawing at arm’s length and asked the three questions out loud. Clear? Yes. Kind? Yes. Done enough to rest?

I waited. The roof was still a little crooked. And I felt the old, familiar pull: just one more line.

“No,” I said, gently, like closing a door. I pressed a tiny gold star sticker into the corner of the paper and turned off the lamp.

It was strange. I did not feel proud or fixed. I felt finished, which turned out to be much better.

At the art fair, Mr. Okafor stopped in front of my lighthouse and said, “I like the little window at the top.” He did not say a word about the roof.

These days, I keep a second card in my drawer: Perfect has no bedtime. I do.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Sunday Night Dread Is Not a Prophecy
articles.summary: Every Sunday at 6:47 a gray feeling announces that Monday will be awful. Lina and Zoe learn to treat it like a weather forecast and build a small “soft landing” for Monday morning.
articles.html:
The dread arrives every Sunday at exactly 6:47 PM, as if it has a bus schedule.

It doesn’t come with a reason. The weekend is still warm, there is still half a pizza in the fridge, and nothing terrible has happened. Yet at 6:47, a gray feeling settles into my stomach and whispers, Tomorrow is going to be awful.

I don’t know what is awful about it. I only know that the feeling is very sure, and it sounds like a weather forecast delivered by someone who has never been wrong.

What if I forgot something for school?

What if Monday goes badly, the whole week goes badly, and I can’t stop it?

Why can’t I enjoy my Sunday?

A forecast is not a prophecy

When I told Zoe, she did not say it was silly. She said, “Oh, I know that one. The Sunday Gray.”

“You get it too?”

“Every week. Mine arrives at five and hangs around until about nine.” She shrugged, the way you shrug when you have lived with a roommate for a long time. “Here’s what I figured out. It’s a forecast. It says cloudy tomorrow. But a forecast isn’t the day. Some days it says storm and I get a bright afternoon.”

I thought about that. The dread was not telling me about Monday. It was telling me about Sunday, about being tired from the weekend and a little sad it was ending. It had borrowed Monday’s name, that was all.

· · ·

The Sunday soft landing

“Okay,” said Zoe. “We don’t fight it. We make a soft landing.”

We wrote the plan on the back of a menu at the bakery, and I kept it afterward.

  1. Pack it now. Bag by the door, clothes on the chair. Fewer surprises for Monday me.
  2. Name the forecast. “This is the Sunday Gray. It is a feeling, not a fact.”
  3. Plant one good thing. Something small to look forward to on Monday morning.

The third one was my favorite. We decided that a good thing did not need to be big. A cinnamon bun. A song I love on the walk to school. A sticker in my notebook that I will find at lunch.

The little star in my pocket

The next Sunday, at 6:47, the gray feeling came right on time. I almost laughed. I said to it, quietly, “Hi, Sunday Gray. I know. You’re a forecast.”

It didn’t go away. But when I did not fight it, it stayed a little smaller. I packed my bag, laid out my clothes, and wrote one thing on a small paper star: cinnamon bun at the bakery. I slid it into the front pocket of my backpack.

On Monday morning, I found the star, and I remembered, and the day started with a small, unexpected smile. Monday was not great. It was not terrible either. It was a normal day, with a math quiz in it and the best cinnamon bun in the world.

The gray still visits. But I don’t think of it as a prophecy anymore. I think of it as the Sunday weather. It rolls in, it rolls out, and tomorrow is its own day entirely.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: Why I Can’t Stop Saying I’m Fine When I’m Not
articles.summary: Lina answers “fine” to everything, even when her chest feels like a storm. Zoe invents the Weather Report, a one-word honest answer that makes telling the truth feel small and safe.
articles.html:
“How are you?” is the easiest question in the world, and I have never once answered it honestly.

“Fine,” I say. Sometimes with a smile, sometimes with a small “good, you?” on top. It comes out of my mouth so smoothly that I don’t even hear it.

That Wednesday, Zoe asked, as she always does, and the word was already halfway out when I noticed that my throat felt tight, my hands were cold, and I had been thinking about the same unfinished message for four hours.

I was not fine. I was a whole drizzly afternoon in a trench coat. But the word was out, and the moment closed over it like water.

Why can’t I just say it?

What if they think I’m dramatic?

What if I say it and it becomes a big thing?

The fine machine

Zoe noticed. Of course she did. She never says much, but she watches closely, the way a person watches a kettle.

“You said fine,” she said later, on the bench behind the gym. “Your shoulders said something else.”

I started to say fine again, and she raised one eyebrow so slowly that I couldn’t help it. I laughed. And then, to my horror, my eyes got wet.

“It’s just,” I said, “fine is easy. If I say anything else, I have to explain it. And I don’t even know what it is.”

Zoe nodded like this was the most reasonable thing she had heard all week. “So don’t explain. Give me the weather.”

· · ·

The weather report

That was how the Weather Report began. Zoe’s rule was simple: instead of “fine,” you give a weather word. Nothing more. No reasons required.

“Sunny,” she said, pointing at herself. “With a chance of tacos.”

I thought about it honestly. It was the first time all day I had actually looked inside.

“Cloudy,” I said. “A little drizzly. Not a storm.”

She nodded, serious, as if I had told her the temperature of a distant planet. “Thanks for the report. Want an umbrella or a snack?”

“…A snack.”

That was all. She handed me half her granola bar, and the tight feeling in my throat loosened by one whole notch. I hadn’t explained anything. I hadn’t become dramatic. I had just told the truth in a very small word, and the world had not ended.

A notebook of small skies

These days, I keep a tiny page called Skies in the back of my notebook. At night I draw the weather of the day: a sun, a gray cloud, a bit of fog. It takes ten seconds. It is the most honest page I own.

And in the daytime, when somebody asks how I am, I try on a new word. Cloudy. Breezy. Foggy but clearing. It surprises me how often people say, “Oh, me too.” Fine, I think, was a door that kept everyone out. A weather word is a window.

I still say fine sometimes. It is a useful word, like a coat that fits in the right weather. But I’ve learned that it is allowed to be one option, not my only one.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Started Before I Felt Ready
articles.summary: A blank sketchbook page waits eleven days for Lina to feel ready. Zoe’s tomato-shaped kitchen timer and a five-minute deal teach her that ready comes from starting.
articles.html:
The sketchbook had been open to the same blank page for eleven days.

It was for the school art fair, and I knew exactly what I wanted to draw. A tall tree, a lantern hanging from a low branch, a little girl underneath it looking up. I could see it perfectly in my head. That was the problem. The picture in my head was beautiful, and anything I made with my hands would be worse.

So I did what any sensible person does. I reorganized my pencils. I cleaned my desk. I made tea, drank half of it, and made another one.

The blank page watched me quietly, the way a dentist watches you pick a magazine.

What if I start and it looks bad?

What if I’m not ready yet?

What if I wait until I feel inspired?

The ready that never comes

“How long have you been getting ready?” Zoe asked, when I told her.

“Eleven days.”

“And how ready do you feel?”

I looked inside. “Less than on day one.”

“Exactly.” She tapped the table with her pencil. “Ready doesn’t come before you start, Lina. It comes from starting. It’s like a bike. You can’t feel balanced while it’s parked.”

I wanted to argue. Instead I said, “But I don’t even know where to begin.”

That was the real sentence, the one I’d been circling for days. And Zoe, for once, did not say anything wise. She just opened her backpack and took out a little round kitchen timer, the kind shaped like a tomato.

· · ·

Five minutes

“This is the deal,” she said, turning the dial. “Five minutes. That’s it. You are allowed to draw badly for five minutes. When it rings, you can stop, and nobody will say a word.”

“What if it’s terrible?”

“Then you’ve made five minutes of terrible, and you can throw it out. Honestly, terrible is still a start.”

I took the pencil. The timer began to tick, loudly, like a very small clock with something to prove. My hand drew a line. It was a crooked line. Then another one. The trunk of the tree came out too thin, and the lantern looked like a lemon.

But something odd happened around minute three. I forgot to judge it. I was too busy fixing the trunk. And when the timer rang, I said, “Wait. Give me a little more.”

“It’s your timer now,” said Zoe, and went back to her sandwich.

Terrible, and mine

I worked for forty minutes that day. The drawing was not the one in my head. It was messier, warmer, and the girl’s face looked slightly surprised, as if she had just heard good news. By the end, I liked it better than the perfect one, because it existed.

Now I keep the tomato timer on my desk. When I notice myself reorganizing pencils, I ask a simple question: Can I do five minutes? I almost always can. And about half the time, I don’t even hear it ring.

My tree hung at the art fair, between a clay mug and a watercolor dragon. The lantern looks a little like a lemon. If you look closely, the girl is smiling.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: What My Body Said When My Mind Wouldn’t Listen
articles.summary: Lina insists she is fine while her stomach knots and her shoulders rise. Zoe calls the body “a very bad texter” and teaches her a gentle check-in: where is it, and what does it need?
articles.html:
My mind said, “I’m not worried about anything.” My stomach said, “Excuse me?”

It happened the morning of the school trip. I had packed my bag, eaten toast, and told everyone I was excited. I really thought I was. Then, on the bus, a hard little knot formed beneath my ribs, my shoulders crept up toward my ears, and my hands started doing a small, nervous dance in my lap.

“I’m fine,” I told my mind. “It’s just a trip.”

My body did not accept this. It kept sending messages anyway: a flutter, a tight jaw, a breath that stopped halfway down. It was like having a very loyal friend who does not speak, only knocks on the wall.

Why does my stomach hurt when nothing is wrong?

Am I sick?

Why can’t I make it stop?

The messenger

I told Zoe at the museum, in front of a very large dinosaur, which seemed appropriate. She listened with her head tilted, and then she said something that I have thought about nearly every day since.

“Maybe your body’s not the problem. Maybe it’s the messenger.”

“The messenger?”

“Your brain says ‘fine,’ your body says ‘not exactly.’ It’s trying to tell you something. Everyone thinks the tummy ache is the enemy, but it’s just very bad at texting.”

I laughed, and the knot loosened, by a hair.

· · ·

Asking the knot

Zoe’s next idea was so simple that I almost refused it. “Put your hand where it hurts,” she said. “Then ask it what it needs. Out loud, if nobody’s watching.”

We walked out to a bench under a big maple tree behind the museum. I put my hand on my stomach, like checking a sleeping cat, and whispered, “What do you need?”

I waited. And, to my great surprise, the answer arrived, in a plain, body sort of language: Water. And to let go of my shoulders.

“Water,” I said. “And I think I’ve been holding my shoulders up for two hours.”

Zoe handed me her bottle. “Okay. Drop them.”

I dropped them. It felt like setting down a suitcase I had forgotten I was carrying.

The check-in

I’d love to say that my stomach never hurts anymore. It does, sometimes, especially before new things. But I have a different relationship with it now. I treat it like a friend with a lot to say, not an enemy to silence.

It goes like this: Where is it? What does it feel like? What does it need? Water, usually. A slow breath. A stretch. Sometimes to say out loud, “I’m a little nervous about tomorrow,” and then it quiets down, as if it just wanted to be heard.

At night, I sit with a warm mug, one hand on my stomach, and I breathe slowly until I can feel the knot unwind, like yarn on a tired cat.

The museum trip, by the way, was wonderful. The dinosaur was enormous. I ate a very good sandwich. And my body, which had warned me to slow down, got to enjoy it too.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Thinking My Friends Were Mad at Me
articles.summary: One letter, “k”, sends Lina into a courtroom of imagined blame. Zoe teaches her to separate what she knows from what she guesses, fill a Maybe Jar with boring reasons, and ask once, kindly.
articles.html:
Sara answered my message with one letter.

I had sent her three sentences, a drawing of a lopsided cat and a heart. It had taken me twenty minutes to make the cat look friendly. She wrote back: k.

No heart. No cat. Not even a period, which somehow made it worse. I looked at that single letter for so long that my phone dimmed itself, politely, as if to give me some privacy.

Then I did what I always do. I started to investigate.

Sara usually sent me three exclamation marks. Sara had not looked up in the hallway that morning. Sara had sat at the far end of the lunch table, holding her tray like a shield. Put together, those facts could only mean one thing: I had done something terrible, and everybody knew except me.

I could not name the terrible thing. That did not slow me down at all. By the time the bell rang, I had built a whole courtroom in my head, and I was the defendant, the judge and the very strict jury.

What did I say wrong?

Is she angry at me?

Does everyone know except me?

The mind is a very bad detective

I told Zoe at the bike racks. I spoke quickly, in one long breath, with the evidence arranged in order.

She did not say, “I’m sure it’s nothing.” She never says that. It sounds kind, but it only makes your brain stand up and argue.

Instead, she asked, “What do you know, and what are you guessing?”

I opened my mouth to say that I knew everything. Then I closed it and thought about it properly.

“I know she wrote k,” I said slowly. “I know she didn’t wave.”

“And the rest?”

“…The rest is a movie I made.”

“Exactly.” Zoe tapped the handlebar. “Your brain is a detective who solves every case with the same answer: it was you. That’s not detective work, Lina. That’s a habit with a magnifying glass.”

I laughed, a little shakily, and something in my chest let go by one notch.

· · ·

The Maybe Jar

That evening, Zoe came over with an empty glass jar and a pad of tiny paper slips. She put them down on my bedroom floor like a doctor setting out instruments.

“New rule,” she said. “For every mad-at-me story, we write three boring reasons. The more boring, the better. Nobody gets to be the villain.”

We sat cross-legged on the rug and wrote them together. Her phone was at 2%. She was hurrying to the dentist. She had a headache and a test. I wrote that she might have been staring at her tray because she was hungry. Zoe wrote that perhaps Sara’s cat had eaten a sock.

It was surprising how easily the reasons came once I stopped trying to be guilty. Each one was dull and ordinary and entirely believable, like a sock-eating cat.

I folded each slip in half and dropped it into the jar. When I shook it, it rattled, a small, plain, reasonable sound. It was the opposite of a courtroom.

Ask once, then wait

“And now,” said Zoe, “the brave part. You don’t guess anymore. You ask. Once.”

We wrote the message together, short and gentle: Hey, I noticed you were quiet today. No pressure, but are we okay? I wanted to add three paragraphs of apology. Zoe held the phone away from me until I agreed to leave it short.

My thumb hovered over send like a bird deciding whether to land. Then I pressed it, turned the phone face down, and went to make tea. That was the second brave part, and honestly the harder one: waiting without checking.

I checked eleven times. I counted. But I checked with the tea in my hand, and that felt like a small victory.

Sara wrote back the next morning, before breakfast.

“OMG I’m so sorry!! I had a migraine all week and my phone was at 2%. I didn’t even see you in the hall, I was squinting at everything. Are WE okay?? Also your cat drawing is the best thing that happened to me all week.”

Underneath, she had added four hearts, a cat and one very small, perfect period.

I laughed until my eyes were wet. The migraine had been in the jar, almost word for word. It was sitting on my shelf, being boring.

What I keep in the jar

I still keep the jar on my shelf. I won’t tell you my brain stopped building courtrooms, because it didn’t. It builds one almost every week, with great enthusiasm and a tiny gavel.

But now I have a routine. I write three boring reasons. I separate what I know from what I guess. I ask once, kindly, and then I wait with my tea.

Most of the time, the answer is a headache, a dead phone, or a tray held too tightly. Sometimes the answer is something real, and we talk about it, and that is fine too. A real problem I can talk about is so much smaller than a courtroom I have to defend all by myself.

My friends were not mad at me. They were just having weeks of their own.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Day I Thought I Was Annoying (I Was Just Tired)
articles.summary: After five hours of sleep and a cracker for breakfast, one small sigh sounds like a verdict. Zoe’s four-question battery check teaches Lina that a tired brain writes terrible reviews, and that verdicts on low battery are not valid.
articles.html:
I said sorry eleven times before lunch, and I had not done anything.

I said sorry to a boy for standing near a door. I said sorry to the librarian for asking a question. I said sorry to my own backpack, quietly, when I knocked it off a chair, and then I wondered if that meant I was losing my mind.

The real trouble began in third period. Our group was planning a science project, and I had a lot of ideas. I explained them quickly, with my hands. Then Tariq sighed, a small, tired, exhale kind of sigh, and looked at the clock.

It was a very ordinary sigh. To me, it sounded like a verdict.

I talk too much. I take over. I am exhausting. Everyone has been politely waiting for me to stop since the fourth grade.

I went quiet for the rest of the class, which felt like the most considerate thing I could do for the world. I wrote nothing on my paper. I wrote annoying in the margin, three times, and then I crossed it out so nobody would see it.

What if everyone is tired of me?

What if I’m too much?

Why can’t I just be easier to be around?

A tired brain writes terrible reviews

Zoe found me on the school steps after class, sitting with my knees pulled up and my chin on my arms. I told her all of it, including the margin.

She listened without saying a word, which is one of her superpowers. Then she asked something I did not expect.

“What time did you go to sleep last night?”

“I don’t know. Late. Maybe one?”

“And when did you wake up?”

“Six. I had to finish the poster.”

“Did you have breakfast?”

I thought about it. “A cracker. I think a cracker.”

Zoe nodded slowly, like a doctor who has finally found the case file. “Okay. So you’ve had five hours of sleep and a cracker, and your brain is now writing a review of your whole personality.”

“It’s not a review,” I said. “It’s the truth.”

“Lina.” She said it very gently. “A tired brain writes terrible reviews. They are always one star. They are always unfair. And they always sound exactly like the truth.”

· · ·

The battery check

Zoe unfolded a tiny sticky note and drew a rectangle with a little bump at one end. It was a battery. She divided it into four sections and labeled them with the smallest handwriting in the world.

“Before you judge yourself,” she said, “you check your battery. Four questions. Slept? Ate? Drank? Quiet? If any of them are empty, you are not allowed to decide anything about yourself. You are only allowed to recharge.”

“What if I do decide?”

“Then you write the verdict down and you reopen the case tomorrow, after a snack and a good night. Verdicts made on low battery are not valid. It’s the law.” She said it so seriously that I laughed, and the laugh surprised me, because I had thought I was too heavy to laugh.

We went to the bakery across the street. Zoe made me eat a whole cinnamon roll and drink an entire glass of water, and for ten minutes we did not talk about anything important at all.

The second review

The next morning, I slept nine hours. I ate eggs and toast. I was, to my great surprise, a person with a normal-sized brain again.

I looked at my notebook margin. Annoying, annoying, annoying, crossed out in angry pen. It looked like it had been written by a stranger who had been up all night, which, in fact, it had.

In class, I braced myself for third period. Tariq came over before it started, and I thought, here it comes.

“Hey,” he said. “Sorry about yesterday. I think I was falling asleep. My little brother had a nightmare and I was up from three. I loved your idea about the plant experiment, by the way. Can we do that one?”

I stared at him. The sigh had been a three AM sigh. It had never been about me.

I stuck Zoe’s battery note on my bedroom wall, next to the lamp. When I notice the old verdict starting, I’m annoying, I’m too much, I check it. Slept? Ate? Drank? Quiet? More often than not, a box is empty, and the verdict can wait.

I still say sorry too much, sometimes. But I’m learning to say thank you for waiting instead of sorry for existing. It turns out those two sentences feel very different in the mouth, and in the chest.

On the days when I really am a bit too loud, I’ve learned something else. People can say so, kindly, and the world doesn’t end. And on the days when I am simply tired, I am allowed to go to bed early and be wrong about myself until morning.

With love,
Lina
