articles.title: How I Learned to Text Without Overthinking for 3 Hours
articles.summary: A four-word invitation takes Lina three hours and fourteen drafts to answer. Zoe’s sticky note, “draft once, read once, send once”, and a sand timer help her send a text that sounds like her.
articles.html:
Noor sent me one question, and I took three hours to answer it.

It was a perfectly lovely question. Want to come to the lake with us on Saturday? Four words, a little sun emoji, no pressure. The kind of message a normal person answers in four seconds with a thumbs-up.

I typed Yes, that sounds great!, and then I stared at it. The exclamation mark felt too excited. I deleted it and wrote Yes, that sounds great. Now it sounded angry. I added a smiley, which looked desperate, and removed it, which looked cold.

I wrote a version with a joke. I deleted the joke because it wasn’t funny enough. I wrote a version with no joke. I deleted that because it was boring. I wrote a draft where I said I might be busy but would try, which was a lie, and then a draft where I explained at length why I was so slow to reply.

By the end of the third hour, I had fourteen drafts. My thumb was sore. My dinner was cold. And Noor, who is one of the nicest people alive, had sent a second message that said only: ?

What if I sound weird?

What if she can tell I’m trying too hard?

What if one wrong word ruins everything?

Nobody reads a text like a judge

I told Zoe the next day, a little ashamed, and showed her the fourteen drafts. She scrolled through them slowly, the way you look at someone’s old holiday photos.

“Draft nine is nice,” she said.

“It’s identical to draft three.”

“I know. That’s the point.” She handed the phone back. “Lina, when you receive a text, do you analyze every comma? Do you hold it up to the light?”

I thought about the messages I get. “No. I read it fast, I feel happy that someone wrote to me, and I forget the words.”

“Exactly. People read your texts the way you read theirs. In one second, with a warm feeling. You’re writing for a judge who doesn’t exist.”

That was surprisingly comforting, and also a little insulting to my fourteen drafts.

· · ·

Draft once, read once, send once

Zoe borrowed a sticky note from my desk and wrote three lines. She stuck it to the back of my phone, where I would have to look at it every time I picked it up.

  1. Draft once. Write it the way you would say it out loud.
  2. Read once. One slow read. Fix only what is unclear or unkind.
  3. Send once. Press send, put the phone face down and go and do something with your hands.

“And one more thing,” she said. “If it takes longer than five minutes, you’re not writing a text anymore. You’re writing a speech for a stranger.”

We tested it right there on the school steps, using a little sand timer from the art room. Noor had just sent a third message: Hope you’re okay! Zoe flipped the timer. I typed Sorry for the late reply, I would love to come on Saturday! What should I bring?

I read it once, aloud, in my normal voice. It sounded exactly like me. I pressed send.

The sand was still running.

The lake, and a face-down phone

Noor replied in nine seconds. Yay!!! Bring snacks!!! We’re leaving at 10.

Three exclamation marks, a sun and a sandwich. That was the whole conversation. It did not contain a single hidden meaning. It was just a friend, glad to hear from me.

I put the phone face down on my desk and made a list of snacks. It was the easiest list I had ever made.

On Saturday, we sat at the edge of the lake with our feet in the water and shared a very squashed bag of pretzels. Noor laughed at something I said without even thinking about it. No one asked me how long my drafts had taken.

I still overthink sometimes. Last week, I caught myself on draft four. I looked at the sticky note on the back of the phone and, with a deep breath, I sent the thing.

It turns out that a text is only a small paper boat. It doesn’t need to be perfect to float. It only needs to be set down on the water.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: Why I Apologize When I Did Nothing Wrong
articles.summary: Lina says sorry to a door, a bus seat and an umbrella. Zoe’s two-question sorry check, “Did I hurt someone? Did I break something?”, helps her save apologies for real moments and say thank you for the rest.
articles.html:
I said sorry to a door this morning.

It was a heavy door, and I pushed it too slowly, and it swung back a little. “Sorry,” I said, to a door, in a voice meant for a very important person.

Then I said sorry to a boy who stepped on my foot on the bus. I said sorry to the driver for asking if this was the right stop. I said sorry to the empty seat beside me, because I had put my bag on it, and for one wild second I thought the seat might be offended.

By the time I reached school, I had counted seven. Not one of them had been my fault.

I did not tell anyone about the sorries. But Zoe was waiting at the gate, and she looked at my face, and she said, “How many so far?”

“How many what?”

“Sorries.”

I stared at her. “How did you know?”

“Lina. You said sorry to my umbrella last week.”

· · ·

The sorry check

We sat on the bench by the bike rack. Zoe took a small card from her pocket, the kind you use for flashcards, and she wrote two questions on it in her round handwriting.

Did I hurt someone?

Did I break something?

“That’s it?” I said.

“That’s it. Sorry is a real word for real moments. If you hurt someone, say it. If you broke something, say it, and offer to fix it. But if the answer to both is no, it’s not a sorry moment. It’s just a moment.”

“Then what do I say?”

She thought about it. “If someone waits for you, say thank you for waiting. If you need help, say excuse me. If you bump a door, say nothing. Doors are very forgiving.”

I laughed, and then I almost said sorry for laughing, and Zoe pointed at the card, and I closed my mouth.

I tucked the card inside my phone case, right where my thumb would find it.

The truth is, I had never asked myself where the sorries came from. Zoe asked me that afternoon, gently, between bites of a pear.

“I think,” I said slowly, “I say it before anyone can be upset with me. Like paying a small fee at the door, so I’m allowed in.”

Zoe stopped chewing. “You don’t have to pay to take up space, you know.”

I looked at my sneakers for a long time. It felt like a tiny window opening in a stuffy room.

· · ·

Seven thank-yous

The next day, I tried it. On the bus, a woman needed to squeeze past, and my old sorry rose up in my throat like a hiccup. I swallowed it, and I said, “Go ahead, take your time.” She smiled and said, “Thanks, sweetheart.”

At the bakery counter, the baker was slow with my change, and I said, “Thank you for waiting on me.” He looked pleased, and he gave me the end piece of the cinnamon bread without my asking.

A few times, the answer was yes. Once, I really did forget to return Zoe’s pencil case, and she had needed it. I said, “I’m sorry. I forgot your pencil case, and I should have brought it back,” and I meant every word. It felt different, solid and clean, like a coin that was worth something.

“See?” Zoe said. “Now it means something. You’ve been saving it.”

I still apologize too much sometimes. Last week, I said sorry to a lamppost, and I told Zoe about it on purpose, and we laughed until our stomachs hurt. But more and more, I find that the thing I wanted to say was thank you, or excuse me, or nothing at all.

It turns out that I am allowed to take up a little space. I do not have to pay at the door.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Learned to Say “No” Without Feeling Guilty
articles.summary: Lina says yes to a big favor before she can think. Zoe’s sticky-note script, “Thank you for asking. I can’t this time,” helps her say a kind no and keep her own evening.
articles.html:
I said yes before Theo finished his sentence.

I was in the school library with five heavy books in my arms, already late for something, and he came over holding a rolled-up map of the whole library. “Could you redo the Autumn Reading display this weekend?” he asked. “Every shelf. It’s a lot, but you’re so good at this.”

My mouth said, “Sure, no problem.” My stomach said something much less polite.

I already had a history project, a cousin’s birthday on Saturday, and a promise to myself that I would sleep like a normal human on Sunday. But Theo smiled, and I felt a small cloud of guilt rise above my head at the very idea of disappointing him. Saying yes felt like paying a bill. Saying no felt like stealing.

That night, Zoe came over with a bag of cookies and took one look at my face.

“You said yes to something you didn’t want to do,” she said.

“How do you always know?”

“Your eyebrows,” said Zoe. “They go up and sad.”

· · ·

The kind no

We sat cross-legged on my bed with tea and a floral pillow between us. Zoe took a yellow sticky note, wrote on it in her round handwriting, and pressed it onto the pillow.

Thank you for asking. I can’t this time.

“That’s a whole no,” she said. “It has a thank-you in front, so it’s polite, and a full stop at the end, so it’s finished. No because, no essay, no tiny apology to the door.”

“But what if he’s upset?”

“Then he’s a person who has feelings about a no, and he’s allowed to. You’re allowed to say it anyway. Guilt is just a smoke alarm, Lina. Sometimes it goes off because of burnt toast, not a fire.”

We practiced. I said it to the pillow, and my voice squeaked on “can’t.” I said it to the lamp. I said it in a dramatic movie-trailer voice, and Zoe laughed so hard she fell sideways into the blankets with a cookie in her hand.

By the end, I could say it with a straight face. Almost.

· · ·

The smoke alarm

The next morning, I found Theo by the shelves. My hands were sweaty. I took a breath, and I said it exactly the way we had practiced.

“Thank you for asking. I can’t this time.”

I waited for the ceiling to fall. It did not. Theo blinked and said, “Oh. Okay! No worries, I’ll ask Marta.” And then he went back to his map as if nothing had happened at all, because for him, nothing had.

The guilt came anyway. It sat on my chest all through math like a small, stubborn cat. I did not argue with it. I told it, “I hear you. You’re a smoke alarm,” and I let it purr until it got bored.

That evening, I did the thing I would have lost on Saturday. I made tea, took one cookie, and spread a big sheet of paper on the kitchen table. I drew stars and hearts and silly squiggles with no reason at all, and I ate the cookie slowly, one bite at a time.

The guilt faded a little more with every star.

I still say yes to plenty of things, and I mean it when I do. But now, before I answer, I try to ask myself one question: if I say yes, what am I saying no to? Sometimes the honest answer is my own Sunday.

It turns out that a kind no is not the opposite of being kind. It is just a yes to something I needed, too.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Tiny Street I Built When My Mind Wouldn’t Stop
articles.summary: Lina’s thoughts swirl like laundry at ten o’clock at night. Zoe gives her a tiny street to build with one rule, “one piece, one breath,” and her busy mind learns to watch instead of run.
articles.html:
My mind did not stop that night. It did not even slow down.

I had a math quiz tomorrow, and a text I had not answered, and a sentence I said at lunch that sounded different in my head now. Each thought was a little cloud, and by ten o’clock there were so many that they began to swirl, round and round, like laundry in a machine.

I sat at my desk with my hands pressed to my temples, as if I could hold my head together. My tea went cold. My notebook stayed open to a page of stars I had drawn instead of studying.

That was when Zoe knocked on my door with a flat box wrapped in a ribbon.

“I can’t take a present right now,” I said. “I can’t think.”

“Good,” said Zoe. “It’s not for thinking. It’s for hands.”

· · ·

One piece, one breath

Inside the box was a tiny street. Not a real one, a kit: little wooden pieces, a bakery with a striped awning, a bookshop with a round window, tiny lanterns, and a pair of silver tweezers no bigger than my finger.

“Here’s the only rule,” Zoe said, tapping a sticky note on my desk lamp. “One piece, one breath. You place one piece, you take one breath. When a thought pops in, you let it float by like a cloud, and you pick up the next piece.”

“And if the thoughts don’t go away?”

“Then you’re building a street with thoughts around. That’s allowed. You just aren’t spinning with them.”

She hugged me, said goodnight, and left me with a lamp, a mug of fresh tea she had slipped onto the desk, and a very small bakery.

The first piece was hard. The tweezers slipped and the wood tilted, and a loud thought said, You can’t even do this. I took one breath. I picked the piece up again. It clicked into place.

The second piece was easier. By the fifth, the swirl above my head had broken into three small clouds. By the tenth, I had forgotten to count.

Somewhere between the bookshop and the lanterns, my shoulders came down from around my ears. My hands knew what to do, and for the first time all evening, my mind was allowed to watch instead of run.

· · ·

A street I did not finish

I did not finish the whole street that night. I built the bakery, the bookshop, a small tree and two lanterns, and then my eyes got heavy.

The math quiz was still tomorrow. The text still needed an answer. But I realized something strange: they were the same size they had been before, only now they were not swirling. They were just things on a list, waiting politely.

Zoe came over the next evening with two mugs of tea and we sat on my bed, looking at the little street glowing on my nightstand. She asked if I was going to finish it.

“Maybe,” I said. “Maybe one piece a night.”

“That’s the whole secret,” she said. “You don’t calm a busy mind by arguing with it. You give your hands something small and kind to do, and your mind follows.”

I answered the text in the morning. I passed the quiz, too, though that part was less dramatic than my brain had promised.

Now, when the clouds start to swirl, I do not try to win. I pick up one tiny piece, and I take one breath.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: How I Stopped Comparing My Inside to Their Outside
articles.summary: Lina thinks Zoe’s life is a sunny meadow while hers is a mess. A room full of tangled cables and forty-one bad photos shows her the trick: she was comparing her inside to Zoe’s outside.
articles.html:
Zoe laughs like sunshine. That is the problem.

She laughs in the hallway, in the cafeteria, in group chats where I only send a heart. She walks into a room as if the room had been waiting for her. And me? I walk into a room and spend the first ten minutes checking which of my hands is more awkward.

One evening I sat on my bed with my phone face down on the pillow, because I had just scrolled through another round of happy pictures. A half-eaten sandwich sat on a plate beside me. My laundry was folded, but only because I had been avoiding something bigger.

In my head, a little cloud floated up. It showed Zoe in a sunny meadow, laughing, with no worries at all. Another cloud showed a perfect cup of tea that nobody had ever spilled.

I thought: Her inside must look like that. Mine looks like this.

That was the whole problem, and I did not see it yet. I was comparing the way I felt on the inside with the way Zoe looked on the outside.

· · ·

The tangled cables

The next afternoon, Zoe invited me to her room to “help with a project.” She wanted to take a photo for the school art board, and she needed someone to hold the tripod steady.

Her room was not the meadow from my cloud. Cables tangled across her desk like spaghetti. Sticky notes fell off the wall. Crumpled photo paper lay all over the floor, and one cushion had a mysterious jam stain.

“I took forty-one photos,” Zoe said cheerfully. “Forty were terrible. One was good enough.”

I picked up one of the rejected photos. It showed Zoe with her eyes closed and her mouth full of cookie. I started laughing, and then she started laughing, and soon we were both on the bed holding our stomachs.

“I get nervous every time I walk into a room,” she said, wiping a tear. “I just walk in anyway. Nobody can see the inside part.”

I stared at her. “You’re nervous?”

“Lina. I rehearsed hello in the mirror this morning.”

And that was the moment the meadow in my head folded up like a paper map. Zoe’s outside was real, and so was her inside, which was messy like mine. I just was not allowed to see it unless she showed me.

· · ·

Inside with inside

Zoe gave me a new rule that afternoon, written on a sticky note in her round handwriting: Inside with inside. Outside with outside.

“If you want to compare,” she said, “compare fair. Your inside to her inside. Or your outside to her outside. Never your inside to her outside. That’s not a comparison. That’s a trick.”

That night, at the kitchen table, I opened a notebook and wrote my own inside page. I wrote that I was nervous in rooms, that I rehearsed hello too, that I sometimes ate a sandwich standing up because I was too tired to sit. I wrote a little, then I wrote a lot, in swirly handwriting that did not even try to be neat.

When I finished, I read it once. It did not look weak. It looked human.

I still scroll sometimes, and the old trick still tries to work. But now I stop and ask: whose inside am I looking at? The answer is always the same. I am not seeing anyone’s inside, and that includes the inside of the girl who laughs like sunshine.

Zoe still walks into rooms as if they had been waiting for her. I know now that her hello was rehearsed, and that makes me like her even more. When I catch myself measuring again, I take a breath and add one more line to my inside page. It is a very small habit, and it is turning out to be one of my favorite ones.

With love,
Lina

articles.title: The Party Where I Thought Everyone Was Judging Me
articles.summary: Lina is sure fifteen people are watching her at an autumn party. Zoe’s spotlight check, counting what she can actually see, shows her a room of people busy with their own worries and cookies.
articles.html:
The party had fairy lights, a table of cookies and about fifteen people. I stood in the doorway holding a mug of tea like a shield.

It was Maya’s autumn party, the kind with pumpkins on the shelves and blankets on every sofa. Zoe had already disappeared into the crowd, laughing. And me? I was holding my mug with both hands, and my mind was already running a very busy movie.

In that movie, every single person was looking at me. They were thinking: Why is she standing there? Why is her sweater so big? Why doesn’t she say something?

I could feel it on my skin, like sunburn. I did not dare to walk in. I did not dare to walk out either.

Then a hand touched my sleeve. Zoe had come back for me.

· · ·

The spotlight check

“Come with me,” she said, and she led me onto the little balcony, where it was quiet and the moon looked like a thumbnail.

“Close your eyes,” said Zoe. “Take a slow breath in. Now, out.”

I breathed. The fairy lights twinkled. Behind the glass door, the party glowed like a snow globe.

“Here’s a game,” Zoe whispered. “It’s called the spotlight check. When you walk back in, you count. Not what you think people are thinking. What you can actually see. How many people are looking at you? And how many are looking at their cup, their phone, or the cookies?”

“What if everyone’s looking?”

“Then you can tell me,” said Zoe, “and I’ll eat a cookie for each one.”

I laughed, a small surprised laugh, and the knot in my chest came a little loose.

“Here’s the secret,” she added. “Everybody at that party thinks they’re the one being watched. Maya is worried about her playlist. Theo is worried about his sleeve. Almost nobody is watching you, because they’re all busy being the main character of their own scary movie.”

· · ·

Counting

When we walked back in, I counted. I really did, in my head, like a tiny scientist.

One person looked at me, and it was Maya, and she smiled and said, “Oh good, you’re here!” Two people were looking at the cookies. Three were arguing happily about which song was best. A boy in glasses was staring at his shoe with great concentration. Nobody was making a face. Nobody was whispering about my sweater.

“Well?” said Zoe, handing me a cookie.

“One,” I said. “And she was friendly.”

“Then I owe you nothing,” said Zoe. “That’s a pity. I wanted ten cookies.”

We sat on the sofa with our mugs, and then somebody told a story about a runaway pumpkin, and I laughed out loud before I remembered to be afraid.

I still feel the old sunburn sometimes, at parties and in the cafeteria. But now I have a game to play. I breathe, I count, and I look at what is actually there instead of the movie.

Most of the time, there is a plate of cookies, a lamp, and a roomful of people who are just as busy worrying about themselves as I am.

With love,
Lina
